messages.author: e358c6bea2b9961c
messages.subject: bilat.symmetry with semilandmarks
parts:
Hi everyone,

I want to investigate the effect of directional symmetry in a dataset of Cetacean skulls. 
I have 51 fixed landmarks and 19 curves, for a total of 339 points (landmarks 52:339 are semilandmarks).

I succesfully ran the bilat.symmetry analysis on the raw data not aligned with the GPA using only the first 51 fixed landmarks, but I am not sure how to do the analysis also including the curves. 

Here is the call I used for the fixed landmarks:
skull_symmetry_all <- bilat.symmetry(shape_array[1:51,,], ind = Ids, object.sym = TRUE, land.pairs = landpairs) 

Looking at the examples, I saw that scallops has 2 extra arguments in the fuction: curves and surface.

Can someone explain to me what those parameters represent so that I can figure out how to obtain them from my dataset?

Thank you, best wishes
Agnese

messages.author: fbfd20ce829c6c6c
messages.subject: Re: [geomorph-r-package] bilat.symmetry with semilandmarks
parts:
Agnese, 

Curves are the 2D semilandmarks, while surfaces are in 3D. Sounds like you are interested in supplying curves. Looking at the scallops curves, we see a matrix where each row corresponds to each sliding semilandmark of interest. For example, row 1 in this matrix corresponds to the instructions for gpagen to slide landmark 6 relative to 5 and 7. Likewise, row 2 tells gpagen how to slide landmark 7, and it is with reference to landmarks 6 and 8. What you need is a similar matrix that identifies all your sliding semilandmarks in the middle column with the "before" and "after" landmarks. This can be made by hand using excel or within R, other software might help automate this "sliders file" too.

Note that the rows do not have to be in numerical sequence (9,10,11 or 10,11,12), it all depends on the order in which you coded your landmarks, in addition to wich landmarks you want to slide relative to. Hope that helps.



Best, 
Bryan

Hi Bryan, 

thank you for your reply. I forgot to mention that my data is in 3D, so I guess I'm looking for a way to supply a surface.
The data for scallops surface is a list of landmarks with one column it seems.

I actually have paired curves on the left and right side of the skull, so I would expect my surface file to have two columns? I would exclude curves that go through the midline. It seems I'm missing something though.

I attach 2 screenshots, first one is obtained by putting all the 3D semilandmarks in 1 column as in the scallops example. Here is the call:

test <- bilat.symmetry(shape_array, ind = Ids, object.sym = TRUE, land.pairs = landpairs, surface = surface) 



In the second I listed the paired semilandmarks on the curves as landmark pairs in the land.pairs argument:

test2 <- bilat.symmetry(shape_array, ind = Ids, object.sym = TRUE, land.pairs = landpairs_surface) 



In this second test the directional asymmetry looks reasonable, but I do not know what is this high level of fluctuating asymmetry.

As I'm only interested in directional asymmetry, is there a way to compare just the symmteric shapes with the DA ones for each specimen?

Thanks a lot, best
Agnese

messages.author: f16866fc42d43e64
messages.subject: Re: [geomorph-r-package] bilat.symmetry with semilandmarks
parts:
Agnese,

I´m afraid the explanation that Bryan gave is partial in a way: the curves argument is for sliding semilandmarks on curves (either 2D or 3D), whereas the surface semilandmarks are for sliders ON SURFACES (which by definition can only be 3D). The scallops dataset has both, being a 3D dataset with both types of sliders.

Now, in your case, you seem to have sliders on curves alone, but in 3D. The definition file would look as Bryan described, and as is defined in the help file of gpagen. The fact that the curves are paired (i.e. symmetric) is a whole different issue, not relevant for how you define the curves and run the initial gpa. Once you have slided the semilandmarks, you would THEN go on and define the paired landmarks (or semilandmarks) and run the bilat.symmetry analysis. So, for bilat.symmetry you need your second solution, but the superimposition would need to be run before that to optimize the positions of the sliders.

Hope this helps,
Antigoni

parts:
Hi Antigoni,

In Cetacea, one group (baleen whales) has a symmetrical skull while the other (toothed whales) have a strong directional asymmetry. This has been shown in several dedicated papers.
Therefore, the "side" argument for baleen whales alone should not be significant. Artificial asymmetry though is causing baleen whales to have a significant side component only when curves are included. Though, when plotting the points, this doesn't show up and it only appears that they have lots of fluctuating asymmetry.

I think part of the issue is also how I import and resample the curves.

Thanks for the explanation of the ANOVA table. I'll look into this and update this thread if I am able to sort this out.

Best,
Agnese
